title: Predappio to Piazzale Loreto: the Duce, the Empire, and the Reckoning
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Dovia di Predappio, the house by the forge
stops.campa: Benito Amilcare Andrea Mussolini is born in two rented rooms above his father's forge at Dovia, a hamlet of the Romagna. Alessandro, a blacksmith and militant internationalist who reads Bakunin between horseshoes, names his son for the Mexican liberator Benito Juárez and for two Italian revolutionaries, Amilcare Cipriani and Andrea Costa. Rosa Maltoni, the schoolteacher mother, is devout where the father is anticlerical; the household is from its first hour divided between the red flag and the crucifix, a division the son will carry and exploit his whole life.
suggested_refs: The Casa Natale di Benito Mussolini at Dovia di Predappio, preserved as a house-museum

stops.name: Predappio, the forge and the socialist hall
stops.campa: As a small boy Mussolini sits among the men at his father's forge and at the local socialist circle, listening to Alessandro read aloud from Il Capitale and denounce priests, landlords and the House of Savoy in the same breath. His mother drags him back to catechism and Mass. He is already known in the village for a temper quick to stones and fists with other boys; neighbors mark him early as clever, unruly and incapable of losing an argument gracefully, a boy already rehearsing for larger stages.
suggested_refs: Alessandro Mussolini's blacksmith forge at Dovia, the boy's first classroom in socialist doctrine
sources: Christopher Hibbert, Benito Mussolini: A Biography (1962)

stops.name: Faenza, the Collegio Salesiano
stops.campa: Sent to board with the Salesian fathers at Faenza, Mussolini chafes under cassocks, bells and corporal discipline he associates with his father's hated Church. In a dormitory quarrel he draws a penknife and wounds a classmate; the incident, and others like it, follow him through more than one Romagnol school before he is finally steered toward the secular Regia Scuola Normale at Forlimpopoli. The pattern that biographers will trace across his whole career, brilliance yoked to violence at the first provocation, is already visible at ten years old.
suggested_refs: The former Salesian college buildings at Faenza, since repurposed
sources: Christopher Hibbert, Benito Mussolini: A Biography (1962)

stops.name: Forlimpopoli, the Regia Scuola Normale
stops.campa: At the state normal school in Forlimpopoli, boarding on a poor scholarship, Mussolini reads Nietzsche, Sorel, Blanqui and Marx alongside the assigned pedagogy texts, already fluent enough in French to translate. He earns his diploma as a certified elementary schoolmaster at seventeen, the one respectable door open to a clever, penniless Romagnol radical. He takes it, but writes even then to friends that ideas, not a blackboard, are his true instrument, and that a small country schoolroom cannot long hold him.
suggested_refs: The Regia Scuola Normale building at Forlimpopoli, where he was certified a schoolmaster

stops.name: Gualtieri, the first schoolroom
stops.campa: Mussolini takes his first post as elementary schoolmaster at Gualtieri in the Reggio Emilia countryside, lodging in a garret and conducting a public love affair that scandalizes the small town's proprieties. He writes fierce anticlerical, antimilitarist columns for the local socialist press in his off hours, already restless in the classroom. Facing the call-up for compulsory military service he despises, he resigns within months and crosses into Switzerland rather than wear the king's uniform.
suggested_refs: Gualtieri's municipal school records of his brief tenure as maestro elementare
sources: Christopher Hibbert, Benito Mussolini: A Biography (1962)

stops.name: Lausanne, arrival and arrest
stops.campa: He arrives in Switzerland with almost nothing, sleeping under bridges and, by his own later account, in an empty barrel by the lakeshore before finding casual work as a stonemason's laborer. On 24 July he is arrested in Lausanne for vagrancy and expelled from the canton, the first of several expulsions that will chase him from canton to canton over the following two years as he agitates among Italian emigrant workers and comes to the attention of the Swiss police as a dangerous foreign radical.
suggested_refs: The Lausanne police vagrancy record of the arrest, 24 July 1902
sources: Swiss National Museum blog, 'Mussolini and Switzerland'

stops.name: Lausanne, L'Avvenire del Lavoratore and Pareto's lectures
stops.campa: Settling enough to write, Mussolini joins L'Avvenire del Lavoratore, the emigrant socialist paper edited by Angelica Balabanoff, who tutors him in German and doctrine and finds his oratory already spellbinding and merciless toward rivals. He audits Vilfredo Pareto's economics lectures at the University of Lausanne, reads voraciously, and crosses paths in the exile cafés with the Russian revolutionaries Lenin and Trotsky, who will recall years later, after his desertion to nationalism, the waste of so vehement a talent lost to the cause.
suggested_refs: L'Avvenire del Lavoratore, the emigrant socialist paper he wrote for in exile

stops.name: Trento, editor for Cesare Battisti
stops.campa: Called into Austrian-ruled Trento by the irredentist socialist Cesare Battisti, Mussolini edits the party's L'Avvenire del Lavoratore and writes for Battisti's own paper Il Popolo, serializing there a lurid anticlerical novel, Claudia Particella, l'amante del cardinale. He agitates openly for Trento's return to Italy, watched now by the Austro-Hungarian police, and finds in Battisti, who will later die on the gallows as a wartime traitor to Austria, a model of conviction backed by the willingness to die for it.
suggested_refs: Il Popolo, the Trento paper edited with Cesare Battisti
sources: Roads to the Great War blog, 'Remembering a Veteran: Cesare Battisti'

stops.name: Trento, expelled from Austria-Hungary
stops.campa: Convicted under the press laws for inciting irredentism, Mussolini is expelled from Austrian territory and marched to the Italian frontier that autumn. He carries out of Trento a personal grudge against the Habsburg empire that intervention propaganda will later put to use, and a taste for exile worn as proof of conviction rather than shame. He settles in September at Forlì to take up the secretaryship of the local Socialist Party section, his name now known well beyond the Romagna.
suggested_refs: The Austro-Hungarian expulsion order against Mussolini, 1909

stops.name: Forlì, La Lotta di Classe and Rachele Guidi
stops.campa: As secretary of the Forlì socialist section Mussolini edits La Lotta di Classe, denouncing Italy's colonial war in Libya and the reformist compromises of the party's moderate wing. He takes as his companion Rachele Guidi, daughter of his father's own mistress, in a Romagnol union at first without priest or magistrate; a daughter, Edda, is born to them that year. His name is now attached, in Socialist Party circles nationally, to the uncompromising revolutionary line against ministerialism and monarchy alike.
suggested_refs: La Lotta di Classe, the Forlì weekly he edited from 1910

stops.name: Milan, editor of Avanti!
stops.campa: At twenty-nine, on the strength of his intransigence at the stormy Reggio Emilia congress that expelled the party's reformist right, Mussolini is named editor of Avanti!, Italian socialism's national daily, and moves it to Milan. Circulation triples under his hand; his columns against the Libyan war and against compromise with the liberal state make him the idol of the party's revolutionary wing and its single most closely watched figure, socialist and prefect alike wondering how far his appetite for confrontation will run.
suggested_refs: Avanti!, the Italian Socialist Party daily he edited from Milan, 1912-1914
sources: TheCollector, 'Benito Mussolini: This Was the Life of Il Duce'

stops.name: Milan, the break over neutrality
stops.campa: As Europe goes to war, Mussolini's editorial of 18 October swings without warning from the party's strict neutrality toward active Italian intervention on the Allied side. Avanti! and the Socialist Party he has served denounce him overnight as a traitor to internationalist doctrine and to every column he has written for a decade. On 20 October he resigns as editor, walking out of the paper that made his name, already certain that the coming trenches, not the picket line, are where history is now being decided.
suggested_refs: Mussolini's editorial 'Dalla neutralità assoluta alla neutralità attiva ed operante,' Avanti!, 18 October 1914
sources: TheCollector, 'Benito Mussolini: This Was the Life of Il Duce'

stops.name: Milan, Il Popolo d'Italia founded, expulsion from the party
stops.campa: With French subsidy and the backing of interventionist industrialists behind him, Mussolini launches Il Popolo d'Italia on 15 November, still subtitled a socialist daily out of old habit. Nine days later a howling party tribunal in Milan expels him for good; former comrades shout traitor and worse as he is driven from the hall he once commanded. He answers them, by several accounts, with a line that becomes legend: they hate him, he says, only because they still love him.
stops.quote: You hate me because you still love me.
stops.quote_source: Socialist Party expulsion tribunal, Milan, 24-25 November 1914 (widely recorded contemporary account)
suggested_refs: The first issue of Il Popolo d'Italia, 15 November 1914
sources: Il Secondo Mestiere, 'Il Popolo d'Italia and great writers-journalists'

stops.name: The Isonzo front, private of the Bersaglieri
stops.campa: Called up with his own class after Italy enters the war in May, Mussolini trains briefly and is sent as a private of the 11th Bersaglieri Regiment to the rock trenches of the Carso above the Isonzo. He keeps a war diary, later published, endures the winter cold, contracts paratyphoid, and is cited for steadiness under fire. The journalist who wrote for months that Italy must fight now lives, without complaint by his own account, in the mud he demanded other men enter.
suggested_refs: Il mio diario di guerra, Mussolini's published wartime diary
sources: Roads to the Great War blog, 'Italy's Elite Bersaglieri'

stops.name: The Carso, wounded
stops.campa: Commanding a trench-mortar section, Mussolini is caught by the accidental detonation of his own unit's bombarda; more than forty fragments of shell tear into his back, legs and side, and he is carried from the line believing himself dying. Surgeons at the field hospital, working without full anesthetic, spend months extracting the metal from his body; he is discharged unfit for further combat and returns to Milan and Il Popolo d'Italia on crutches, the wound already folding itself into the legend he is building.
suggested_refs: The forty-four shell fragments removed from Mussolini's body after February 1917
sources: Today in World War I, 'Mussolini Gravely Wounded'

segments.name: The Fasci and the Black Squads

stops.name: Milan, Piazza San Sepolcro, the founding of the Fasci
stops.campa: In a hall of the Circolo dell'Industria e del Commercio on the Piazza San Sepolcro, before some hundred and fifty restless veterans, Arditi, futurists and revolutionary syndicalists, Mussolini founds the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento. The San Sepolcro program is a chaos of anti-plutocratic and nationalist demands, a republic invoked in one clause and the monarchy left standing in the next, unresolved and unresolvable. Within months the black-shirted squadre it spawns will say plainly, with club and petrol, what the manifesto only hints.
suggested_refs: The Fascist Manifesto (San Sepolcro Programme), published in Il Popolo d'Italia, 6 June 1919
sources: Wikipedia, Fasci Italiani di Combattimento; Fascist Manifesto
Carmilla Online, '23 marzo 1919: genesi e primi passi del fascismo'

stops.name: Milan, watching Fiume fall
stops.campa: When Giolitti's regular army shells Gabriele d'Annunzio's occupied Fiume at Christmas to force the poet-commander out under the Treaty of Rapallo, Mussolini, who has praised the Fiume enterprise in Il Popolo d'Italia and quietly borrowed its balcony harangues, its black shirts, its Roman salute, sends no men and no guns to save it. He watches from Milan a rival cult of personality broken in five days by the very state he means one day to seize for himself, and studies the lesson without evident regret.
suggested_refs: The balcony, salute and black-shirt liturgy of Fiume, adopted wholesale into Fascist ritual
sources: dannunzio.journey.json (the Natale di sangue, shared frame)
Dublin Review of Books, 'The Fascist Precursor'

stops.name: Ferrara and the Po valley, the squadre
stops.campa: Across the Po valley the squadre, financed by agrarian landowners frightened of the red leagues and cooperatives, purge village after village with the manganello, forced castor oil and the torch, burning chambers of labor and party halls. At Ferrara in February the method is perfected and copied everywhere within weeks. Mussolini, still publicly for legality and a return to constitutional order, does not command each raid but rides the wave the squadristi raise, disciplining a scattered terror into the instrument that will take Rome.
suggested_refs: The manganello (billy club) and forced castor oil, signature instruments of squadrismo
sources: Cambridge Core, 'Paramilitary Violence and Fascism: Imaginaries and Practices of Squadrismo, 1919-1925'
Foundation for the History of Totalitarianism, 'Mussolini and his thugs'

stops.name: Milan, elected to the Chamber
stops.campa: After fascism's null result in the 1919 elections, Mussolini remakes tactics, running on Giolitti's National Blocs list; in the general election of May he wins a parliamentary seat from Milan, entering the very chamber his own squadristi terrorize in the streets outside. It is a double strategy, ballot alongside bludgeon, that the old liberal establishment, confident it can absorb and tame fascism through office, fails to see for what it truly is until the strategy has already succeeded.
suggested_refs: The 1921 Italian general election results, Mussolini's first parliamentary seat
sources: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Mussolini Seizes Dictatorial Powers in Italy'

stops.name: Rome, the Third Congress, the National Fascist Party founded
stops.campa: At the Third Fascist Congress in Rome the loose, contradictory Fasci are reorganized into the Partito Nazionale Fascista, with Mussolini installed as Duce and a program tilted now toward order, the monarchy and reconciliation with the Church rather than the old republican syndicalism of San Sepolcro. The movement trades ambiguity for discipline and street violence for party structure; the year that follows will show how much of a shaken Italy is ready to make the same trade.
suggested_refs: The founding statute of the Partito Nazionale Fascista, Rome, November 1921

stops.name: Naples, the congress and the cry of 'a Roma!'
stops.campa: At the Fascist congress in Naples, before tens of thousands of blackshirts massed in the Piazza del Plebiscito and the San Carlo theater, Mussolini all but announces the coup to come: either the government is handed to fascism, he cries, or fascism will seize it by descending on Rome. The crowd answers with the chant that gives the coming days their name. Within hours the quadrumvirate is organizing columns of squadristi from every province to converge on the capital.
stops.quote: Either they give us the government, or we will seize it by marching on Rome.
stops.quote_source: Speech at the Fascist Party congress, Naples, 24 October 1922
suggested_refs: The 'a Roma!' chant at the Naples congress, 24 October 1922
sources: War History Online, 'The March on Rome and Benito Mussolini's Quest'

stops.name: Rome, the March and the appointment as prime minister
stops.campa: While some thirty thousand ill-armed squadristi camp outside a capital the regular army could easily have scattered, King Victor Emmanuel III refuses to sign Prime Minister Facta's decree of martial law. On the 29th he summons Mussolini to form a government; Mussolini travels overnight from Milan by sleeper-train and arrives the morning of the 30th in a black shirt among the frock coats of the Quirinal, sworn in as the youngest prime minister in the kingdom's history. The march itself follows him into Rome afterward, a parade of the already victorious.
suggested_refs: Mussolini's overnight train from Milan to Rome, 29-30 October 1922
sources: World War II Day by Day, 'Benito Mussolini and His Fascists Spark Riots'

stops.name: Rome, the Acerbo Law
stops.campa: With fascism holding barely a third of the Chamber, Mussolini pushes through the Acerbo Law: whichever list wins at least a quarter of the national vote takes two-thirds of the parliamentary seats outright. Liberal deputies who imagine they are taming an ambitious minister into constitutional habits vote it through. In the April 1924 election, held under a hail of squadrist intimidation, the government list duly claims its supermajority, and parliament signs away, by its own hand, the mechanism that might have checked the man it still calls prime minister.
suggested_refs: The text of the Acerbo Law, approved 21 July 1923
sources: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Mussolini Seizes Dictatorial Powers in Italy'

stops.name: Rome, Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, the Matteotti kidnapping
stops.campa: Days after denouncing the fraud of the April election from the floor of the Chamber and promising documents that will prove worse, the Socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti is seized on the Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia and bundled into a waiting Lancia by five men of the Fascist Ceka. He is beaten unconscious and driven off toward the Ponte Milvio; his body will not be found for two months, buried in a shallow grave in woods outside the city. Mussolini denies all knowledge, but the killers trace back into his own inner circle.
suggested_refs: The Monument to Giacomo Matteotti on the Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, Rome
sources: libcom.org, '10 June 1924: The murder of Giacomo Matteotti'
TheCollector, 'The Murder That Nearly Toppled Mussolini'

stops.name: Rome, the Chamber, the Aventine Secession
stops.campa: Some hundred and thirty opposition deputies, Socialists, Popolari and Liberals together, walk out of the Chamber in what will be called the Aventine Secession, refusing to sit again beside men implicated in Matteotti's murder until the king dismisses Mussolini. They wait on constitutional propriety and royal conscience; neither arrives. By emptying the one chamber that might have restrained him, the boycott instead hands Mussolini the year of relative quiet he needs to close every remaining door behind it.
suggested_refs: The Sala della Lupa, Montecitorio, where the seceding deputies met

stops.name: Rome, the Chamber, the speech that begins the dictatorship
stops.campa: Before a Chamber still half in shock, Mussolini ends six months of crisis at a single stroke: he alone, he declares, assumes the political, moral and historical responsibility for everything that has happened, dares the deputies to impeach him, and promises the country will be set in order within forty-eight hours. Within days opposition newspapers are shut, meeting halls sealed, over a hundred dissidents arrested. The speech is remembered ever after as the true founding date of the Fascist dictatorship.
stops.quote: I declare here, before this Assembly and before the entire Italian people, that I alone assume the political, moral, and historical responsibility for everything that has happened.
stops.quote_source: Speech to the Chamber of Deputies, Rome, 3 January 1925
suggested_refs: The full text of the 3 January 1925 speech, entered in the parliamentary record
sources: History.com, 'Benito Mussolini declares himself dictator of Italy'
FIRSTonline, 'Mussolini's Speech That Started the Fascist Dictatorship'

stops.name: Rome, the Lateran Palace, the Pacts signed
stops.campa: At noon in the Lateran Palace, Mussolini for the Kingdom of Italy and Cardinal Gasparri for Pope Pius XI sign the treaty, concordat and financial convention that close the fifty-nine-year Roman Question. Vatican City is recognized as a sovereign state the size of a park; Catholicism is restored as Italy's state religion. The Church that once excommunicated the men who took Rome from the Pope now blesses the regime that rules it; church bells ring across the peninsula, and the once fiercely anticlerical Duce is hailed by the faithful as a man of Providence.
suggested_refs: The Lateran Treaty, signed 11 February 1929, ending the Roman Question
sources: Papal Artifacts, 'The Signing of the Lateran Treaty on February 11, 1929'

stops.name: Littoria, the battle of the marshes and the wheat
stops.campa: On the reclaimed Pontine Marshes, drained at last of the malarial water that has ruled this coast since Roman times, Mussolini inaugurates the new town of Littoria, raised by decree in under eight months. He poses shirtless with a scythe for the newsreel cameras of the wheat battle, threshing grain beside veteran settler-families each given a farmhouse, a cow and a plough. It is fascism's proudest boast of creation rather than conquest, though the older wetland life of the coast disappears beneath the new farms.
suggested_refs: LUCE newsreel footage of Mussolini threshing wheat, bare-chested, in the Pontine reclamation
sources: Environment & Society Portal, 'Circeo National Park: Fascist Land-Reclamation'

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Venezia, war declared on Ethiopia
stops.campa: From the balcony of the Palazzo Venezia, before a piazza packed and relayed by radio across the whole peninsula, Mussolini announces the invasion of Ethiopia, an old colonial grudge dressed as civilizing mission and answer to League of Nations sanctions he calls an unjust siege of a proud people. Within hours Marshal De Bono's forces cross from Eritrea. Over the following months, on Mussolini's own written authorization, mustard gas banned by treaty since 1925 will be dropped on Ethiopian troops and villages alike to break a resistance the conventional advance cannot.
suggested_refs: The balcony of the Palazzo Venezia, site of Mussolini's great public declarations

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Venezia, the empire proclaimed
stops.campa: Addis Ababa fallen and Haile Selassie fled into exile, Mussolini returns to the same balcony to proclaim the birth of the Italian Empire: Victor Emmanuel III is hailed Emperor of Ethiopia, Badoglio made Duke of Addis Ababa, and Mussolini himself takes the title First Marshal of the Empire. Enormous crowds, primed by fifteen years of propaganda, roar their approval below him. It is the zenith of his popularity, the hour Fascist Italy believes it has truly refounded Rome.
stops.quote: After fifteen centuries, the empire reappears on the fateful hills of Rome.
stops.quote_source: Balcony address, Palazzo Venezia, Rome, 9 May 1936
suggested_refs: Newsreel footage of the 9 May 1936 empire proclamation, Palazzo Venezia balcony

stops.name: Milan, Piazza del Duomo, the Axis speech
stops.campa: Speaking in Milan on the anniversary of the March on Rome, Mussolini names the new understanding with Nazi Germany, agreed weeks earlier, an axis around which the rest of Europe might yet be induced to revolve, not a diaphragm dividing the continent but a line of collaboration open to all. The word outlives the speech and gives the coming alliance its name. He still imagines Italy the senior, civilizing partner in the pairing, steering an ally rather than serving a master, an illusion the following nine years will strip from him piece by piece.
stops.quote: This Berlin-Rome line is not a diaphragm but rather an axis around which all those European states with a will to collaboration and peace can also assemble.
stops.quote_source: Speech in the Piazza del Duomo, Milan, 1 November 1936
suggested_refs: The word 'Axis,' coined in this speech, naming the alliance for the rest of history

stops.name: Rome, the Manifesto della razza and the racial laws
stops.campa: To prove Fascist Italy's loyalty to its German ally, Mussolini's government publishes the Manifesto della razza, declaring Italians a race apart and the country's Jews foreign to the Italian nation. Through the autumn the racial laws follow, stripping Italian Jews, among them decorated veterans and party members of the first hour, of citizenship, property, profession and schooling. Mussolini, who had mocked Nazi race theory as recently as a few years before, signs the laws that make Fascist Italy an active partner in Hitler's antisemitism rather than its reluctant guest.
suggested_refs: The Manifesto della razza, published in all national papers, 14 July 1938
sources: Jerusalem Post, 'Mussolini's Jews: How Il Duce bewitched Italy's Jewish communities'

stops.name: Munich, the four-power conference
stops.campa: Summoned by Chamberlain's plea and Hitler's threat of war over the Sudetenland, Mussolini proposes a four-power conference and flies to Munich to broker it, arriving as the one man both Hitler and the Western democracies will still hear. The agreement drafted overnight, and signed by Hitler, Chamberlain, Daladier and himself, hands Hitler the Sudetenland without a shot fired. He returns to a Rome that cheers him in the streets as the savior of European peace, a peace that will not survive another twelve months.
suggested_refs: The Munich Agreement, signed 30 September 1938 at the Führerbau

stops.name: Rome, awaiting the Pact of Steel
stops.campa: While Ciano and Ribbentrop sign in Berlin, Mussolini waits in Rome for word of the alliance he has named himself, discarding his first choice, Pact of Blood, for the harder-edged Pact of Steel. The treaty binds Italy to support Germany in any war it starts, offensive or defensive, with no exit clause and no requirement of consultation. Mussolini privately tells his own generals Italy will not be ready for a general war before 1943 at the earliest, a caveat Hitler will not trouble himself to honor.
suggested_refs: The Pact of Steel, signed in Berlin, 22 May 1939
sources: History.com, 'The Pact of Steel is signed; the Axis is formed'

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Venezia, the declaration of war
stops.campa: With France already beaten and Britain apparently soon to follow, Mussolini judges the moment safe to enter a war he fears missing rather than one he is prepared to fight. From the Palazzo Venezia balcony he tells the massed crowd that an hour marked by destiny is striking in the sky of the fatherland, the hour of irrevocable decisions. The army he sends within weeks against a collapsing France, and soon after into Greece and North Africa, will expose within months how little of the imperial machine built through the 1930s was ever real.
stops.quote: An hour marked by destiny is striking in the sky of our fatherland. The hour of irrevocable decisions.
stops.quote_source: Declaration of war, Palazzo Venezia balcony, Rome, 10 June 1940
suggested_refs: The only filmed declaration of war of the Second World War, 10 June 1940
sources: Historical Resources About the Second World War, 'Mussolini: Speech of the 10 June 1940'
Human Touch Media, 'Mussolini Declaration of War'

stops.name: Rome, the Grand Council, the Grandi motion
stops.campa: With Sicily invaded and Rome itself bombed for the first time, the Fascist Grand Council meets for the first time in years through the night of the twenty-fourth into the early hours of the twenty-fifth. Dino Grandi's motion, asking the king to resume full constitutional command of the armed forces, passes nineteen votes to seven after nine exhausting hours in which Mussolini argues but does not fight. He leaves believing the vote merely advisory to the crown. It is, in law and in fact, the instrument by which his own creature ends twenty-one years of dictatorship.
suggested_refs: The roll-call vote of the Grand Council of Fascism, night of 24-25 July 1943
sources: Wikipedia, Fall of the Fascist regime in Italy

stops.name: Rome, Villa Savoia, the arrest
stops.campa: Summoned that afternoon to Villa Savoia expecting a routine audience, Mussolini is told by Victor Emmanuel III that the war is lost, that Marshal Badoglio will form the next government, and that he is, in the king's own words, the most hated man in Italy. Stepping outside in a daze after twenty minutes he is stopped by carabinieri, bundled into a Red Cross ambulance under armed guard, and driven away into a captivity that will move him from barracks to island to mountain over the following seven weeks.
suggested_refs: Villa Savoia (now Villa Ada), site of the audience and the arrest, 25 July 1943
sources: Wikipedia, Fall of the fascist regime in Italy

segments.name: Gran Sasso and the Republic of Salò

stops.name: Campo Imperatore, the Gran Sasso rescue
stops.campa: Held now at the Hotel Campo Imperatore high on the Gran Sasso, reachable only by cable car, Mussolini watches German gliders crash-land on the mountain plateau below the hotel windows. A hundred SS troopers and paratroopers under Otto Skorzeny overwhelm the guard without a shot fired, and Mussolini is flown out in a tiny Storch aircraft that barely clears the cliff edge on takeoff. He is not a free man returning to power but a rescued prisoner, and both he and Hitler already know which of the two states now truly owns the other.
stops.quote: I knew that my friend Adolf Hitler would not abandon me.
stops.quote_source: Attributed by Otto Skorzeny, Skorzeny's Special Missions (1950)
suggested_refs: The Hotel Campo Imperatore, its terrace where the gliders landed
sources: TheCollector, 'How the Nazis Rescued Benito Mussolini'

stops.name: Rastenburg, East Prussia, meeting Hitler at the Wolfsschanze
stops.campa: Flown by way of Vienna and Munich to Hitler's forest headquarters in East Prussia, Mussolini meets the ally who ordered his rescue and now dictates his future. Hitler wants a Fascist government restored in the German-occupied north to hold Italy in the war and shield the Reich's exposed southern flank. Mussolini, sick, visibly aged, and without an army, an illusion, or any real choice left him, agrees to head the state Hitler names for him, no longer a sovereign ally but an instrument of the occupying power.
suggested_refs: The Wolfsschanze (Wolf's Lair), Hitler's Eastern Front headquarters
sources: Swiss National Museum blog, 'The rescue of Benito Mussolini'

stops.name: Gargnano, Palazzo Feltrinelli, the Republic proclaimed
stops.campa: The Italian Social Republic is proclaimed, its ministries scattered in towns around Lake Garda, its nominal capital the small lakeside town of Salò, though Mussolini himself lodges and works under permanent SS guard at the requisitioned Villa Feltrinelli in Gargnano. He revives on paper the old syndicalist program of 1919, land and factories promised to the workers in a socialization decree meant to prove fascism was never merely capital's servant, even as German officers and Italian partisans in the surrounding mountains decide the republic's real business without consulting him.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Feltrinelli at Gargnano, seat of the Salò government's councils of ministers
sources: Il Post, 'La nascita della Repubblica di Salò'

stops.name: Verona, Castelvecchio, the trial and Ciano's execution
stops.campa: At Castelvecchio a special tribunal tries the Grand Council members who voted against him the previous July, among them his own son-in-law Galeazzo Ciano, husband of his daughter Edda. Found guilty of treason in a proceeding whose verdict is fixed before it opens, Ciano and four others are shot in the fortress ditch on the eleventh of January, tied to chairs and shot in the back by the executioners' own choice of humiliation. Edda's plea for clemency, smuggled out with Ciano's diaries as her price, reaches Mussolini's desk one day too late, by design; he lets the sentence stand.
suggested_refs: The Ciano diaries, smuggled to Switzerland by Edda Mussolini Ciano as the price of a clemency plea
sources: Executed Today, '1944: Galeazzo Ciano and four other Italian Fascists'

stops.name: Dongo, the capture
stops.campa: As the Republic collapses and Milan's partisans rise, Mussolini flees north toward Switzerland or the Alps within a retreating German convoy, Claretta Petacci following in a car of her own. At Musso a roadblock of the 52nd Garibaldi Brigade stops the column; the next morning at Dongo a searching partisan recognizes the unmistakable jutting chin of a soldier slumped in a greatcoat among the German trucks. We have got Mussolini, the cry goes up along the lakeshore; twenty-one years of dictatorship end at a fuel-truck checkpoint on the road to Como.

sources: War History Online, 'How Did Benito Mussolini Die?'

stops.name: Giulino di Mezzegra, Villa Belmonte, the execution
stops.campa: Held overnight with Petacci at a farmhouse above Bonzanigo, Mussolini is brought down the following afternoon before the gate of Villa Belmonte by partisans acting, they say, on the National Liberation Committee's order. He and Petacci are shot against the villa's low stone wall; accounts of his final seconds disagree, some claiming he bared his chest and asked to be struck there, others that no words passed between the condemned and their executioners at all. The bodies are loaded that night, with others shot the same day, onto a truck bound for Milan.
suggested_refs: The stone wall of Villa Belmonte at Giulino di Mezzegra, site of the execution
sources: All That's Interesting, 'The Grisly Story Of Benito Mussolini's Capture, Execution, And Defilement'

stops.name: Milan, Piazzale Loreto, the bodies displayed
stops.campa: Before dawn the bodies of Mussolini, Petacci and fifteen other executed fascists are dumped in the Piazzale Loreto, the same square where fascist militia had left the bodies of fifteen executed partisans on public view the previous August. The crowd that gathers through the morning kicks, spits on and mutilates the dead Duce; by afternoon he and Petacci are strung up by the feet from the girders of a bombed Esso filling station, an image that closes, for the world's cameras, twenty-three years of Fascist Italy.
